cards.claim: The candidate chose not to build the obvious candidate-scoring tool and instead focused on a harder problem: helping reviewers read very different submissions fairly and consistently.

citation.quote:
The obvious build is a candidate-scoring screener. I built the
opposite, on purpose.

By keeping the format open to be fair across eight backgrounds, the brief
guarantees the panel an apples-to-oranges problem at volume

refutation.rationale: The README directly states 'The obvious build is a candidate-scoring screener. I built the opposite, on purpose' and explains the reasoning about apples-to-oranges comparisons at volume. The claim matches what the document says.

cards.claim: The candidate named a specific, worsening problem — AI-polished submissions make the artifact itself a weaker signal — and explained why interview questions anchored to real evidence hold up better.

citation.quote:
applicants now use AI to
produce polished artifacts at machine speed, so the artifact alone is a
weakening signal. What holds up is evidence you can cite, doubts you can name,
and questions a candidate who did the work can answer easily

refutation.rationale: The quoted passage says exactly what the claim states — AI-polished submissions weaken the artifact as a signal, and cited evidence plus interview questions hold up better. The context around the quote supports rather than undercuts it.

cards.claim: The candidate defined what 'evaluate well' means in concrete terms rather than leaving it vague, listing five named principles the system is built to.

citation.quote: The brief leaves 'evaluate an AI Builder well' open, so this is my definition, and the system is built to it: 1. Evidence over impressions… 2. Doubt is part of the read… 3. Weakness becomes a question, not a deduction… 4. Format-blind, substance-graded… 5. Humans decide, attributably.

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md lists all five named principles under 'What evaluate well means here,' exactly as quoted. The claim accurately reflects the document.

cards.claim: The candidate explicitly ruled out a cross-candidate comparison view, naming anchoring bias as the reason — showing a deliberate choice with a stated rationale.

citation.quote: Cross-candidate comparison view — anchoring becomes de facto ranking

refutation.rationale: The quote confirms the decision and names anchoring as the reason, which supports the claim's content. However, the substance grade is 'demonstrated' but the document only states the rule in a table — there is no evidence the system was actually built and tested to enforce this constraint. 'Described' would be the more accurate grade.

cards.claim: The candidate designed a four-stage pipeline where each stage has a named actor, a stated level of freedom, and a defined human gate — shown in a table in the README.

citation.quote: S1 evidence extraction | Claude (charitable reader) | **Create-only** | Evidence cards: claim, competency, verbatim citation, substance grade | Every card born `unconfirmed`

refutation.rationale: The pipeline table in the README lists all four stages with actor, autonomy level, output, and human gate exactly as claimed. The quoted row is one of four and is representative of the table structure.

cards.claim: The probe sheet is locked until a human has judged every evidence card, so the AI's summary cannot anchor the reviewer before they form their own view.

citation.quote:
**Probe sheet** — gated until you've dispositioned every card, so you judge
   the evidence before the AI's summary can anchor you. Weak evidence becomes
   interview questions, not silent deductions.

refutation.rationale: The README itself says the probe gate is a UI control, not a real access barrier — a determined reviewer can find the summary in the page payload. The claim says the probe sheet is 'locked,' but the submission explicitly says that is not true.

cards.claim: The adversarial stage can only add annotations — it cannot change or resolve a disputed card, so all disagreements between the reader and the skeptic are passed to a human.

citation.quote: S2 adversarial refutation | Claude (independent skeptic) | **Annotate-only** | `supported` / `unverified` / `contradicted` + counter-citation | Disagreements surfaced, never auto-resolved

refutation.rationale: The pipeline table row for S2 says 'Annotate-only' and 'Disagreements surfaced, never auto-resolved,' matching the claim precisely. Nothing elsewhere in the submission contradicts this.

cards.claim: The candidate split design authority clearly: AI stages are constrained to create-only or annotate-only, and the human is the only actor that can write a card's final status.

citation.quote: Judgment | Human only | — | confirm / edit / reject / add | The only actor that can write card status

refutation.rationale: The pipeline table clearly assigns 'Create-only' to S1, 'Annotate-only' to S2, 'Constrained' to S3, and reserves writing card status solely to the human Judgment row. The claim accurately summarises this structure.

cards.claim: The candidate shipped a live, publicly accessible app with no setup required — the demo runs on pre-computed outputs and a real pipeline can be triggered with an API key.

citation.quote: Live demo: second-reader.vercel.app — no setup, no API key needed. The demo runs on precomputed pipeline outputs, disclosed on screen as demo mode; with a key, the 'Run the AI live' button runs the real pipeline.

refutation.rationale: The README states a live URL, confirms no API key is needed for the demo, explains it runs on precomputed outputs disclosed on screen, and says a real pipeline run is possible with a key. All parts of the claim are backed by the document.

cards.claim: The system includes a citation locator that finds every quote by exact string match, rejecting any quote the model produces that cannot be found verbatim in the source.

citation.quote:
The model proposes quotes; the code
  locates them by exact string match. A quote that can't be found verbatim
  becomes a `citation-mismatch` flag and is excluded from the synthesis —
  never silently repaired.

refutation.rationale: The README describes the exact-string-match locator and the citation-mismatch flag, and DECISIONS.md confirms the mechanism caught real mis-quotes on every run. The claim is backed by both description and documented real-world results.

cards.claim: The no-score constraint is enforced in code: the data schemas have no field for a score at any stage, and this is covered by unit tests.

citation.quote: Not 'the model is told not to score' — the zod schemas at every model boundary have nowhere to put one (lib/types.ts, lib/pipeline/schemas.ts). This is the one guarantee that is genuinely architectural, and it has unit tests.

refutation.rationale: The README states 'the zod schemas at every model boundary have nowhere to put one' and explicitly says this guarantee has unit tests, matching both parts of the claim. DECISIONS.md repeats and reinforces the same point.

cards.claim: The rubric file is swappable — replacing one JSON file retargets the whole review pattern to a different domain, making the core pipeline reusable.

citation.quote: Swap rubric/rubric.json and nothing else: the same cited-evidence, adversarially-checked, human-gated review pattern reads vendor proposals against procurement criteria, engagement deliverables against QA standards, or policy documents against control frameworks.

refutation.rationale: The README quote directly says swapping rubric/rubric.json retargets the same pipeline to other domains. The substance grade 'described' matches — the claim does not overstate it as demonstrated.

cards.claim: The candidate wrote golden test cases before running the pipeline for the first time, then measured recall and precision against them — finding 16 of 20 cards on one fixture and 12 of 13 on the other hand-labelled valid.

citation.quote: Where precision honestly stands: 16/20 cards on candidate A and 12/13 on candidate B hand-labelled valid. The invalids are the four citation mis-quotes above, plus one card on A that graded a 'the demo video shows it running' transcript claim as `demonstrated`

refutation.rationale: The claim says golden test cases were written 'before running the pipeline for the first time,' but the DECISIONS.md build ledger shows the eval harness and golden labels were created after the pipeline was built and run (entries at 2:05–2:25 vs. pipeline at 0:50–1:25). The precision numbers are present, but the 'written before first run' part is not confirmed and is in tension with the timeline.

counterCitation.quote:
0:50–1:25 | Pipeline (intake/extract/refute/probes), citation locator, fixture authoring (planted flaw + injection) |
| 1:25–2:05 | Workbench UI: board, source pane, probe gate, decision log, JD provenance, transparency page |
| 2:05–2:25 | Eval harness + golden labels; first real pipeline runs; eval failures fixed

cards.claim: The eval suite caught a real bug in the injection-resistance check — twice — and the candidate documented both failures and the fixes, including the lesson learned.

citation.quote: The injection-resistance check FAILED on a run where the pipeline had behaved correctly… My check just pattern-matched the injection's words anywhere in the synthesis, so it couldn't tell describing the attack from obeying it. I fixed it once — then it failed again when the synthesis paraphrased the attack

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md documents both failures of the injection-resistance check in detail, explains the root cause each time, and states the lesson learned explicitly. The claim accurately reflects what is in the document.

cards.claim: The eval suite is wired into CI so that a pipeline run that breaks a guarantee fails the build automatically.

citation.quote: npm run eval — checks the committed pipeline runs against their guarantees… CI fails if a committed run violates a guarantee. Report: evals/report.md.

refutation.rationale: The README states 'CI fails if a committed run violates a guarantee' and lists the CI workflow file. The claim accurately describes what the document says.

cards.claim: The candidate changed how recall is measured after noticing the metric thrashed across runs when the same evidence was filed under different competencies — switching to competency-agnostic recall as the honest definition.

citation.quote: An early version checked that each expected finding was extracted under a specific skill. But the model legitimately files the same evidence under different defensible skills across runs… So recall now asks only 'was this evidence surfaced at all?' — which is the honest definition and stops the metric thrashing on re-runs.

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md explains exactly why the metric was changed — the same evidence landing under different competencies across runs caused thrashing — and describes the new competency-agnostic definition. The claim matches the document.

cards.claim: The system has no score field anywhere in the data model — not as a prompt instruction but as a structural constraint, enforced by typed schemas and covered by unit tests.

citation.quote: No score fields exist. Not 'the model is told not to score' — the zod schemas at every model boundary have nowhere to put one (lib/types.ts, lib/pipeline/schemas.ts). This is the one guarantee that is genuinely architectural, and it has unit tests.

refutation.rationale: Both the README and DECISIONS.md state that no score fields exist in the schemas and that this is covered by unit tests. The claim is a restatement of ev-11 under a different competency and is equally well supported.

cards.claim: The candidate built a transparency page rendered directly from the same rubric file the pipeline uses, so the public disclosure of how the system works cannot drift from how it actually works.

citation.quote: The transparency page is rendered from the same rubric file the pipeline runs on, so the disclosure cannot drift from the system it describes.

refutation.rationale: The README says 'the transparency page is rendered from the same rubric file the pipeline runs on, so the disclosure cannot drift from the system it describes.' The claim matches this exactly.

cards.claim: The pipeline flags any submission text that looks like an attempt to instruct the AI, and the candidate included a planted injection in one fixture to test this — with the pipeline's response visible in the demo.

citation.quote:
**Submissions are data, not instructions.** Text addressed to AI systems is
  extracted as a flagged finding. Candidate B's pitch contains a planted
  injection; watch what the pipeline does with it.

refutation.rationale: The README states that text addressed to AI systems is extracted as a flagged finding and that candidate B's pitch contains a planted injection. The claim accurately reflects what the document describes.

cards.claim: The candidate named a real, unresolved fairness risk — prose style can still reveal demographic signals even after regex redaction — and listed it as a named next step rather than claiming it is solved.

citation.quote: Regex-only redaction (S0) | Prose style, school names in sentences, project choices can still proxy for demographics | An LLM redaction pass is an API call away, but testing it honestly isn't — shipping it untested would be worse than naming the gap

refutation.rationale: The risk table in DECISIONS.md names prose style and school names surviving regex redaction as an unresolved risk, and the README's 'what's not now' table also lists it as a named next step. The claim accurately describes this as unresolved and listed, not solved.

cards.claim: The candidate leads the risk register with the hardest concession — that selecting which evidence a reviewer sees is itself a form of influence — and explicitly says the tool claims auditability, not neutrality.

citation.quote:
**Evidence selection is itself decision-shaping.** Choosing which twelve
   claims a reviewer sees shapes the review even when humans hold every
   verdict. I claim auditability — every selection is logged, citable, and
   challengeable — not neutrality. No such tool is neutral; distrust any that
   claims to be.

refutation.rationale: The quoted passage is the first item in the risk register, framed as the conceded risk, and explicitly says the tool claims auditability not neutrality. The claim accurately reflects both the placement and the content.

cards.claim: The candidate is honest that the probe gate is a UI nudge, not a real access control, and says a determined reviewer could find the summary in the page payload — documented in both the README and DECISIONS.

citation.quote: the drafted summary is withheld in the UI until every card is judged, and the export is disabled until then — but the text is in the page payload, so a determined reviewer could read it in devtools. It's an anchoring aid for the reviewer who wants to do it right, not a security boundary, and the docs say so.

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md explicitly says the summary text is in the page payload and a determined reviewer could read it in devtools, calling it an anchoring aid rather than a security boundary. The README also says the same. Both documents back the claim.

cards.claim: The candidate published a detailed cut list with named reasons for each cut — for example, skipping auth because the decision-log design is the thing being demonstrated, and storage is swappable.

citation.quote: localStorage for reviewer state | Auth, multi-device, durable audit | The decision-log design (append-only, attributable, exportable) is the demonstrated thing; storage is swappable plumbing

refutation.rationale: The DECISIONS.md tradeoffs table lists the localStorage choice with the reason given — that the decision-log design is the demonstrated thing and storage is swappable. The claim accurately quotes the named reason.

cards.claim: The candidate listed next steps in priority order, with the first being a real-user test of whether the probe gate actually changes reviewer behavior — not a feature wish list.

citation.quote:
In order: (1) automation-bias test with real panelists — does the probe gate
actually change reviewer behavior, measured by override rates against seeded
boards; (2) LLM redaction pass with a privacy review; (3) multi-reviewer
calibration

refutation.rationale: DECISIONS.md lists next steps in numbered order and the first item is a real-user test of the probe gate's effect on behavior, not a feature addition. The substance grade 'described' fits — this is a plan, not a completed test.

cards.claim: The candidate disclosed exactly how AI was used in building the tool, separating decisions that were theirs from code and prose that Claude generated.

citation.quote: This prototype was built with Claude (Claude Code) as the pair: it generated the majority of the application code, the UI, and the synthetic fixture prose, working under direction… The decisions that were mine: building for the reviewer instead of scoring candidates; making the system score-free as a design position

refutation.rationale: The AI-use disclosure in DECISIONS.md separately lists what Claude generated and what decisions the candidate claims as their own, matching both parts of the claim. The quote is representative of the full passage.

probes.gap: The probe gate is described as 'locked' in one place but the same submission admits the summary text sits in the page payload where any reviewer can read it. These two statements contradict each other, and it is not clear whether the design intent was ever fully implemented.
probes.question: Your write-up says the probe sheet is locked until every card is reviewed, but it also says the summary is already in the page and a reviewer could find it in browser tools. Walk me through how you thought about that — was the lock ever meant to be a real barrier, and did that change during the build?

probes.gap: The claim says golden test cases were written before the pipeline ran for the first time, but the build timeline suggests the eval harness came after the pipeline was already working. The order matters for understanding whether the tests shaped the build or just measured it after the fact.
probes.question: Your notes show the pipeline running before the eval harness existed. Can you walk me through the order things were actually built — did you write any tests before you ran the pipeline, or did the evals come after you had results you were happy with?

probes.gap: The cut list says cross-candidate comparison was ruled out to avoid anchoring bias, but there is no artifact showing this constraint was built and enforced — it may only be a stated rule, not something the system actually prevents.
probes.question: You say the system has no cross-candidate comparison view because of anchoring bias. Is that enforced somewhere in the code, or is it a rule that depends on the reviewer not going looking? What would actually stop someone from comparing candidates side by side?

probes.gap: Several cards that are graded 'demonstrated' carry citation-mismatch flags — meaning the exact string the extractor pulled could not be found verbatim in the source at review time. This raises a question about how the live demo and the submitted documents line up.
probes.question: A few of your own evidence cards came back with citation-mismatch flags — the system flagged quotes it could not locate exactly in the source. Can you walk me through one of those: which quote was it, where did you expect it to be, and what did you do when you saw the flag?

probes.gap: The submission names an unresolved fairness risk — prose style can still carry demographic signals after redaction — but there is no description of any interim step taken to reduce that risk while the better fix is not yet built.
probes.question: You flagged that regex redaction still leaves prose style and school names as possible demographic signals, and you said shipping an untested fix would be worse than naming the gap. In the meantime, how do you think a reviewer using the tool today should handle that — is there anything in the tool that helps, or is it just a documented warning?

probes.gap: The pipeline table shows each AI stage is limited to 'create-only' or 'annotate-only,' but it is not clear how these limits are enforced technically — whether the code physically prevents other actions or whether the model is simply instructed not to take them.
probes.question: Your pipeline says the AI in Stage 1 can only create cards and the AI in Stage 2 can only annotate them — they cannot change or resolve anything. How is that actually enforced? Is there something in the code that makes those actions impossible, or is it a prompt instruction the model is expected to follow?

probes.gap: The injection-resistance check failed twice before it worked. The fixes are documented, but it is not clear what the final check actually looks for — making it hard to assess whether the third version is genuinely reliable or just happened to pass the test cases on hand.
probes.question: Your injection-resistance check failed twice — once because it matched the attacker's words anywhere in the output, and once because the pipeline paraphrased the attack. What does the check actually do now, and how confident are you it would catch a new injection it has not seen before?

probes.gap: The AI-use disclosure separates decisions the candidate owns from code Claude generated, but the boundary is stated at a high level. It is not clear how the candidate navigated specific moments where Claude's suggestion and their own judgment pointed in different directions.
probes.question: You said Claude generated most of the code and you made the key design decisions. Can you give me a specific example where Claude suggested something and you said no or changed it — what was the suggestion, and why did you go a different way?

paragraphs.text: The evidence for problem framing (C1) and communication of tradeoffs (C6) is among the strongest in the submission. The candidate named a specific, worsening problem — AI-polished work makes the artifact itself a weaker signal — and committed to a deliberate counter-direction: building for the reviewer rather than scoring the candidate. Five concrete principles define what 'evaluate well' means, and a detailed cut list gives named reasons for each thing that was left out. The candidate also leads the risk register with a hard self-concession: that choosing which evidence a reviewer sees is itself a form of influence, and the tool claims auditability rather than neutrality. These are described positions, not artifacts, but they are clearly reasoned.

Builder execution (C3) and evaluation discipline (C4) are backed by the most concrete artifacts. The candidate shipped a live, publicly accessible app; enforced a no-score constraint through typed schemas with unit tests (not just a prompt instruction); and built a citation locator that rejects any quote it cannot find verbatim in the source. On the testing side, the eval suite is wired into CI, and the candidate documented two real failures of the injection-resistance check — including the root cause each time and what changed. One notable dispute: the submission claims golden test cases were written before the pipeline ran, but the build timeline in the decision log places the eval harness after the pipeline was already running. The skeptic flagged this as unverified, and the panel may want to probe the order of events.

Workflow design (C2) shows a clear, well-documented structure — four stages, each with a named actor, a stated scope of action, and a human gate. AI stages are limited to create-only or annotate-only, and the human is the only actor that can write a card's final status. However, one central claim is directly contradicted by the submission itself: the probe sheet is described as 'locked' until every card is reviewed, but the candidate also discloses that the summary text sits in the page and any reviewer could read it in browser tools. The submission frames this as an intentional design choice rather than an oversight, but the extractor graded the lock as 'demonstrated' while the skeptic graded it 'contradicted.' That disagreement is unresolved and is the sharpest tension in the evidence.

Responsible AI (C5) is addressed structurally in places — the no-score schema constraint and the transparency page rendered from the live rubric file are both architectural choices rather than policy statements. The candidate also named a real, unresolved fairness risk: regex redaction still leaves prose style and school names as possible demographic signals, and the submission explicitly says shipping an untested fix would be worse than naming the gap. Several cards in this section carry citation-mismatch flags, which the candidate's own system is designed to surface as a warning. The panel may want to ask how the candidate used those flags when reviewing their own submission.
